The equity ratio stood at 25.2%, a figure that, while still modest by Japanese industrial standards, represented a materially healthier balance sheet than the negative equity territory of eighteen months prior.

The market's reaction was extreme. Shares that had languished in the ¥150–¥200 band through most of the second half of 2025 broke out decisively: the trajectory ran from ¥247 to ¥369, then ¥564, ¥922, ¥1,072, ¥1,372, ¥1,792, ¥2,192 — each leg accompanied by volume spikes that in the peak week exceeded 50 million shares daily, against a pre-restructuring norm of roughly 300,000–500,000. The stock hit an intraday high of **¥4,380** sometime in the March–April 2026 window, implying a market capitalisation that the underlying earnings — ¥9.0 billion in nine months annualises to roughly ¥12 billion — struggled to justify at any conventional multiple.

An [April 6, 2026 press release](https://www.unitika.co.jp/news/io-pdf/re20260406-02.pdf) appears to have been a secondary catalyst, though the PDF binary was not parsed in the research pipeline and its precise content remains unverified here.

## What the ¥1,574 Close Implies

By May 22, 2026, the stock had retraced to ¥1,574 — still roughly ten times the ¥145 trough, but 64% off the peak. The correction reflects a familiar dynamic in distressed-turnaround trades: the first profitable quarters get priced at growth-stock multiples, and when the growth rate inevitably moderates — or when the next catalyst (full-year results, Tusco Thailand divestiture, a semiconductor glass-fiber design win announcement) fails to materialise on schedule — the multiple compresses sharply.

Three forward catalysts will determine whether ¥1,574 represents base or dead-cat-bounce: closure of the Tusco Thailand manufacturing transfer (which would complete the geographic retreat and free remaining cash), incremental glass-fiber design wins in semiconductor packaging applications (where the per-substrate economics are orders of magnitude better than apparel-grade fiber), and the FY3/26 full-year results due May 2026. The last item lands inside the frozen window and may already be public — but its contents, and whether operating momentum held through Q4, remain the unresolved question hanging over every valuation exercise in this dossier.

chapters.title: Patents, products, and the case for specialty pricing
chapters.body:
## The arithmetic of specialty

Unitika spent ¥2,965 million on research and development in the fiscal year ended March 2025, down from ¥3,461 million two years earlier, according to company financials compiled by [Stock Analysis](https://stockanalysis.com/quote/tyo/3103/financials/). As a share of the ¥126.4 billion in FY3/25 revenue, that is roughly 2.3 percent — a thin figure by the standards of specialty-materials peers, and a declining one at precisely the moment Unitika is staking its future on hard-to-replicate polymer and glass-fiber know-how. Whether the portfolio is genuinely IP-dense or merely IP-adjacent matters enormously for the credibility of the ¥6.5 billion operating-profit target (9.3% margin) the company has set itself for FY3/29.

The honest answer is: it depends on which product you look at.

## UniPeel: contamination-free at 180°C

The clearest example of defensible IP is [UniPeel](https://www.unitika.co.jp/film/e/products/unipeel/), Unitika's silicone-free release film for semiconductor and electronics processing. Conventional release films deposit trace silicone contamination on substrates — tolerable in consumer applications, disqualifying in capacitor and PCB manufacture where silicone can cause delamination and adhesion failures. UniPeel substitutes a proprietary silicone-free coating that maintains stable peel force from ambient temperature up to 180°C across three commercial grades (Grade I through III), and is chemically resistant to toluene, MEK, and ethyl acetate — the solvents common in epoxy and polyimide coating lines.

The application set — process film for substrates and capacitors, cover film for flat-panel displays, transfer foils — tracks almost precisely with the semiconductor-packaging supply chain that is growing fastest in Japan. Unitika's own segment commentary for the nine months to December 2025 flags "electronic-materials demand" as the primary driver of industrial-film growth within the ¥42.5 billion Polymers segment. No production volumes or unit pricing are disclosed, so the revenue contribution of UniPeel specifically is opaque. But the direction of customer pull is unambiguous.

## EMBLEM HG: boil-and-retort as a moat

In food packaging, Unitika's flagship IP story is [EMBLEM HG](https://www.unitika.co.jp/global-packaging-film/products/emblem-hg/), a high gas-barrier biaxially oriented polyamide film whose oxygen-barrier performance *improves* after boiling and retorting — a counter-intuitive property rooted in how the nylon coating restructures under thermal stress. Unitika traces the EMBLEM line to the world's first simultaneous biaxial-orientation method, commercialised in 1968; the HG grade extends that lineage into barrier-functional coatings suited for retort pouches, vacuum-packed ready meals, and microwaveable packaging.

EMBLEM-HG is explicitly named in the nine-month segment review as a contributor to Polymers' 67% year-on-year operating-profit surge. Food-grade nylon film for retort applications is not commodity polyester: converters require validated barrier performance across sterilisation cycles, and switching suppliers triggers requalification. That switching cost is a soft form of IP protection that doesn't show up in patent counts.

## Glass fibers: the AI infrastructure bet

The Performance Materials segment's glass-fiber sub-business has quietly become one of Unitika's more interesting AI-adjacent positions. The nine-month commentary describes "significant" growth in electronic-materials glass fabrics, specifically citing "ultra-thin Low CTE Glass Fabrics" and "ultra-thin E Glass Fabrics" adopted by manufacturers of high-end mobile memory. Low-CTE (low coefficient of thermal expansion) glass cloth is the reinforcing skeleton inside ABF and BT substrates — the laminated platforms that sit between logic dies and PCB in advanced packaging architectures like CoWoS. As die stacking and chiplet integration intensify, substrate warpage control becomes a gating factor; low-CTE fabric is a direct enabler. Unitika filed a glass cloth and glass yarn patent (JP7017214B1) covering this area in 2021, suggesting at least some registered protection around yarn construction. The company notes an integrated production chain from yarn-drawing through surface treatment as a barrier to fast imitation.

## The DIC partnership: borrowed credibility

The strongest external validation of Unitika's polymer IP came in October 2024, when DIC Corporation — a ¥1 trillion speciality-chemicals group — [announced](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20241009429520/en/DIC-and-Unitika-Collaborate-to-Develop-a-Specialty-PPS-Film-with-Low-Dielectric-Properties-Suitable-for-Use-in-a-Key-Material-for-Millimeter-Wave-Printed-Circuit-Boards-and-Millimeter-Wave-Radar) a joint development programme with Unitika on polyphenylene sulphide film for millimetre-wave applications (30–300 GHz). DIC contributes PPS polymerisation and compounding; Unitika contributes film-manufacturing process. The resulting film suppresses transmission loss at high frequencies, addressing a gap where conventional liquid-crystal polymer films underperform. By December 2025, DIC was showcasing the collaboration at CES 2026. Counterparties at this scale do not co-develop with suppliers they regard as technically marginal.

## The margin gap

The 9.3% operating margin target for FY3/29 is achievable — but it is not a specialty-materials margin. [High-IP specialty film makers such as Toray Advanced Film or Toyobo's film division run operating margins in the 12–15% range](https://www.trendforce.com/news/2025/11/24/news-what-is-glass-fiber-fabric-and-why-is-t-glass-critical-for-ai-servers-a-deep-dive/) when the mix skews toward functional coatings and electronic applications. Unitika's blended result will be held down by the glass-beads sub-segment (losing to offshore price competition), declining commodity polyester staple, and the residual Fibers & Textiles segment that contributed only ¥50 million in operating profit on nearly ¥24 billion of revenue in the first nine months of FY3/26.

| Segment (9m FY3/26) | Revenue ¥B | OP ¥B | OP margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| Polymers | 42.5 | 7.5 | 17.8% |
| Performance Materials | 29.1 | 1.4 | 4.9% |
| Fibers & Textiles | 23.9 | 0.05 | 0.2% |

The Polymers segment already operates at margins consistent with a specialty film business. The drag is everywhere else. The FY3/29 plan essentially requires either Performance Materials to reach a similar profile — which demands that the glass-fiber and activated-carbon-fiber sub-segments win further electronic-materials share — or for Fibers & Textiles to shrink far enough to stop diluting the blended average. Both are in motion; neither is complete. At ¥2.97 billion in annual R&D spend on a revenue base that will contract toward ¥70 billion by FY3/29, the company will need every patent it holds to earn its keep.

chapters.title: What could break this
chapters.body:
The turnaround math works — but only if roughly a dozen things go right simultaneously. Unitika's operating profit swung from ¥-2.5B in FY3/24 to ¥9.0B in the nine months through December 2025, and the capital adequacy ratio recovered from a precarious 10.4% to 25.2% after the REVIC injection. The problem is that each pillar of that recovery carries a specific failure mode, and several of them are correlated.

## The Unsold Anchor

The most visible loose end in Unitika's divestiture programme is TUSCO, the Thailand polyester spunbond operation the company has been trying to sell since at least mid-2025. As of [October 2025](https://www.nonwovens-industry.com/breaking-news/unitika-seeking-buyer-for-nonwovens-business/), it remained without a buyer. Management has set aside roughly ¥6B for demolition and wind-down costs should no acquirer materialise — a figure that sits uncomfortably against the ¥5.9B full-year operating profit Unitika posted in all of FY3/25. A forced closure rather than a sale would consume most of one year's earnings, potentially trigger fresh impairment charges on top of the ¥37.9B already taken in FY3/25, and signal to the market that the divestiture programme is moving on the company's timeline, not management's.

The broader restructuring also generated ¥12.4B in restructuring charges in the nine-month period alongside ¥23.7B in asset-sale gains — the net is flattering, but the gross numbers show how much capital is still being consumed to exit legacy positions. Every month TUSCO remains on the books, it ties up management attention and carries operating risk in a commodity market where Unitika has already decided it cannot compete.

## Designed-In, Designed-Out

The high-margin part of the story — ultra-thin Low CTE Glass Fabrics for mobile memory substrates, UniPeel silicone-free release films for semiconductor processing, the joint PPS film development with DIC Corporation for millimetre-wave radar — depends entirely on Unitika's products surviving the qualification process at a small number of sophisticated manufacturers. The segment commentary for Performance Materials notes that "electronic materials grew significantly" in the nine months through December 2025, but ¥1.44B operating profit on ¥29.1B revenue is a 4.9% margin: the segment is not yet generating returns that justify the concentration risk.

Qualification cycles in semiconductor packaging are long and sticky once won, which is the bull case. But Toray and Teijin — both significantly larger, both with established relationships at the same customers — can absorb the development cost of entering Unitika's specialty corners if the pricing signal is strong enough. Unitika's five-year plan targets ¥70B revenue by FY3/29, down from ¥126B today, which implies a company that becomes heavily dependent on a narrow band of high-value applications. If even one design win at a major memory or substrate manufacturer is lost to a Toray alternative, the growth narrative for the company's most strategically important segment cracks before it has been validated by sustained margin delivery.

## The REVIC Clock

REVIC holds 66.76% of voting rights via Class C preferred shares issued on 30 April 2025. Its annual preferred dividend is ¥2.27 per share — negligible in absolute terms. The strategic risk is not the dividend; it is the exit. REVIC's mandate as a state-backed restructuring vehicle is to recapitalise distressed companies and then disengage. When it does — whether through conversion to common, a block sale to a strategic acquirer, or a buyback by Unitika — the overhang on common stock could be substantial. Common shareholders currently have no dividend (¥0 forecast for FY3/26) and no clear timetable for when REVIC's position resolves.

The governance tension compounds this. President Fujii Minoru, 63, is a career Unitika employee appointed in April 2025, self-described as "the only career employee in management." The reconstituted board has seven outside directors — a condition of the REVIC capital injection — meaning the people closest to Unitika's operational history have the least formal power, while REVIC's nominees hold the votes. Who actually drives strategy between a career-insider CEO executing a roadmap designed under duress and a state-backed majority shareholder with its own exit incentives is not resolved in any public document.

## Currency and Everything Else

The nine-month results included a ¥940M foreign-exchange valuation gain driven by yen depreciation. That contribution disappears — and reverses — if the yen strengthens. Unitika's cost base is predominantly yen-denominated; its revenue mix includes meaningful export and overseas exposure. The asymmetry is uncomfortable: yen weakness helped Q3, but yen strength would squeeze margins in a company still thin enough that the Fibers and Textiles segment earned only ¥50M operating profit in nine months.

The company's own Q3 commentary flagged "uncertainties in trade policy, exchange rate fluctuations, and geopolitical risks including Japan-China relations." Each maps onto a specific exposure: US tariff escalation disrupts the electronics supply chain that buys Unitika's high-value films and glass fabrics; yen volatility directly hits reported profitability; and Japan-China tension threatens both the agricultural and industrial nonwovens markets where Chinese competition is already eroding glass-bead pricing. None of these is unique to Unitika, but a company with a 10% capital buffer as recently as March 2025 and a stock that traded between ¥140 and ¥4,380 over the past 52 weeks has much less cushion to absorb macro shocks than its larger peers.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The immediate horizon: a full-year report card due now

The frozen snapshot date of 22 May 2026 lands almost exactly at Unitika's full-year reporting window. Japanese fiscal-year companies typically release annual results in mid-to-late May; Unitika published its FY3/25 full-year disclosures on 14 May 2025. Full-year FY3/26 results — covering the twelve months ended 31 March 2026 — are therefore either days away or already in print. That makes the first catalyst question simple: does the company hit its February 2026 revised guidance of ¥110,000M revenue, ¥9,500M operating profit, and ¥20,000M net income?

The answer, almost certainly, is yes on profit — and the maths are not close. Nine-month operating profit through December 2025 already reached ¥9,030M, leaving the full-year target requiring only ¥470M from the January-March quarter. That is a ¥470M bar for a quarter whose trailing nine-month pace was running at ¥1,003M per month. Either guidance was deliberately sandbagged, or something went materially wrong in Q4. The more interesting question is how far above the ¥9,500M line the final print lands — and what that implies for FY3/27 credibility.

Revenue is trickier. The ¥110,000M guidance represents a -13% decline from FY3/25's ¥126,400M, almost entirely driven by the divestiture of spinning, garment technology, and the Indonesian trading entity. Nine-month revenue of ¥95,637M (+2.2% organic) suggests full-year revenue lands close to guidance — ¥110,000M requires ¥14,363M in Q4, which is plausible given the seasonally stronger January-March quarter for packaging films.

## The quarterly catalyst map: June 2026 – May 2027

| Quarter | Approximate Date | Key Event |
|---|---|---|
| FY3/26 full year | May 2026 | Annual results; FY3/27 guidance issued |
| AGM / board reconstitution | 26 June 2026 | Kashiwagi steps to part-time; Furukawa retires; Hakomori joins |
| FY3/27 Q1 | ~August 2026 | First clean quarter; polymer and glass-fiber volume trends |
| FY3/27 H1 | ~November 2026 | Mid-year check on operating margin trajectory |
| FY3/27 Q3 (9M) | ~February 2027 | Guidance revision or reaffirmation; glass-fiber design-win visibility |
| FY3/28 preview | May 2027 | Full-year FY3/27 results; medium-term trajectory reset |

The board transition on 26 June is a governance event with financial implications. Kashiwagi Hisami — REVIC's deployed Managing Director — moves from executive vice-president to part-time non-executive director. The rationale given in the April 2026 announcement was that "business recovery plan [is] progressing smoothly; structural reforms largely complete; enabling new management to focus on growth strategy." That language is PE-template boilerplate for "the restructuring operator is leaving." What it does not resolve is what REVIC itself plans to do with its 66.76% voting stake in Class C preferred shares.

## Guidance and the implied growth rates

Management has published a five-year target for FY3/29: ¥70,000M revenue and ¥6,500M operating profit. Set against FY3/26 guidance of ¥110,000M / ¥9,500M, that implies revenue declining a further -36% over three years and operating profit falling -31% in absolute terms — even as operating margin improves modestly from 8.6% to 9.3%.

This is not the growth story the stock price implies. A five-year target that shrinks both revenue and absolute profit in exchange for slightly better margins is a contraction-with-discipline plan, not a recovery-and-scale plan. Investors bidding the stock to ¥1,574 — a 902% recovery from its market-cap trough — are paying 45x trailing earnings for a company whose own five-year plan shows declining absolute profits.

No external analyst consensus is available in the prep data, but the internal math is illustrative. If FY3/26 full-year net income lands near ¥20,000M (as guided, boosted by one-time asset-sale gains of ¥23,661M and a ¥940M FX valuation gain), then the FY3/27 comparison year strips those one-time items and normalises. Recurring operating profit of ¥9,500M in FY3/26 converting at a roughly 30-35% effective tax rate implies normalised net income somewhere in the ¥6,000–7,000M range — which, against 57.65M common shares, suggests underlying EPS of ¥104–121 per share. At ¥1,574, that is a 13–15x multiple on clean earnings — not obviously cheap for a restructuring-phase specialty-materials company with no common dividend.

## The dilution trap every common holder must price

The nine-month disclosure prints basic EPS of ¥184.72 alongside diluted EPS of ¥20.49 — a ratio of roughly nine to one. That gap is not a footnote; it is the core structural risk for common shareholders. On a fully diluted basis, REVIC's Class C preferred instruments convert into equity at terms set during the company's distressed nadir, implying an effective diluted share count roughly nine times the 57.65M common shares outstanding. If and when REVIC monetises its position — whether by converting Class C to common and selling, by arranging a block trade, or by requiring Unitika to redeem — common shareholders face severe dilution or an overhang that suppresses the price for years. Management has made no public statement about the REVIC exit timeline.

## What to watch, quarter by quarter

**FY3/26 full year (May 2026 release):** The hard data points are operating profit versus the ¥9,500M guide and the composition of the ¥20,000M net income target. Stripping the ¥23,661M gain on asset sales and the ¥940M FX gain from the nine-month extraordinary items, the underlying recurring earnings picture is what matters. A beat on operating profit that is driven by polymer-film margin expansion is bullish; a beat driven by additional asset-sale gains is not.

**Glass fiber as the leading indicator:** Performance Materials segment operating profit grew 251.7% in nine months to ¥1,441M on revenue of ¥29,144M. The sub-segment commentary identifies "ultra-thin Low CTE Glass Fabrics + ultra-thin E Glass Fabrics for high-end mobile memory" as the growth driver. This is an AI-adjacent exposure — advanced packaging substrates for HBM and high-density DRAM require precisely the kind of low-coefficient-of-thermal-expansion glass fabric Unitika supplies. The metric to watch is whether this sub-segment maintains its growth rate into the memory-capex cycle of calendar 2026. A slowdown in orders from major Korean or Taiwanese memory fabs would hit this number in Q1 or Q2 FY3/27.

**Polymer segment margin sustainability:** Polymer operating profit ran at ¥7,543M for nine months, an operating margin of roughly 17.8% — exceptional for a film converter. The commentary flags nylon and polyester packaging films and EMBLEM-HG (a high-barrier film used in food packaging) as drivers. Margin durability depends on resin input costs and packaging-end-market pricing. A resin spike or pricing pressure from Korean/Chinese competitors would compress this rapidly.

**FY3/27 guidance issuance:** The single most important data point in the next twelve months is what management guides for FY3/27 — the first year without one-time divestiture gains, without Kashiwagi's scaffolding, and with the smaller consolidated perimeter fully embedded. If FY3/27 guidance comes in above ¥9,000M operating profit on roughly ¥85–90B revenue (the logical midpoint between FY3/26 actuals and the FY3/29 target trajectory), it validates the restructuring thesis. If guidance implies operating profit below ¥7,000M, it confirms that the FY3/26 numbers were heavily inflated by cost-reduction windfalls that won't repeat.

## The asymmetry

The bull setup is coherent: a company that was operationally loss-making three years ago is now generating ¥9,500M operating profit on a cleaner portfolio, has rebuilt equity from ¥15,568M to ¥45,472M in twelve months, holds ¥57,956M in cash (four times the year-ago level), and has two technically differentiated businesses — polymer packaging films and glass fabrics for advanced electronics — with secular demand tailwinds. If glass-fiber design wins for AI memory substrates scale, the Performance Materials segment alone could approach ¥3,000M operating profit within two years.

The bear setup is equally coherent. The stock has already priced a full recovery — from ¥127 to ¥1,574 is a 12x move over five years, and the current P/E of 45x rests on earnings heavily inflated by one-time gains. The five-year plan targets smaller absolute profits. Common shareholders hold minority governance rights under REVIC's 66.76% voting control, receive no dividend, and face potential nine-fold dilution if Class C converts at distressed-era pricing. The succession question — whether Fujii, Misu, Kobayashi, and Fujimoto can execute a specialty-materials growth strategy without the restructuring scaffolding REVIC provided — is entirely unproven. Beta of 2.03 and a 52-week range of ¥140 to ¥4,380 says the market already knows this is a high-variance instrument. The next twelve months will determine whether the variance resolves upward on glass-fiber volumes and margin durability, or downward on REVIC dilution mechanics and a guidance reset that strips the one-time shine from FY3/26's headline numbers.

chapters.title: What to watch for next
chapters.body:
## The Calendar That Matters

Unitika's first real verdict arrives in May 2026, when the company publishes its FY3/26 full-year results against guidance of ¥110 billion in revenue and ¥9.5 billion in operating profit. After nine months, the company has already booked ¥95.6 billion in revenue and ¥9.0 billion in operating profit — meaning the implied fourth quarter needs to contribute only ¥0.5 billion more on the operating line. That looks deliberately conservative. What analysts should read carefully is the composition: how much of that final-quarter operating profit comes from ongoing operations versus one-time restructuring gains, which ran ¥23.7 billion on the nine-month extraordinary income line.

The full-year net income guidance of ¥20 billion, against a nine-month actual of ¥10.6 billion, implies a heavy-back Q4 on the bottom line — consistent with deferred divestiture-related gains. If those closings slip into FY3/27, the headline net income number will miss even if operating performance is solid.

## Green Lights

Three events would confirm the restructuring thesis more than any earnings beat.

First: closure of the Tusco Thailand divestiture. The spinning and weaving operations that bled the old Fiber segment for years — operating loss of ¥357 million in FY3/25 on ¥33.9 billion in revenue, barely 0.8% growth — need to be contractually off Unitika's books. The company set August 2025 as its internal deadline for agreeing all structural-reform divestitures; any slippage into the back half of FY3/27 would signal that asset buyers are not accepting Unitika's price expectations.

Second: sustained double-digit revenue growth in EMBLEM HG and UniPeel barrier films within the Polymers segment. In the nine months to December, Polymers posted ¥42.5 billion in revenue and ¥7.5 billion in operating profit — an operating margin of 17.7%, far above the company average. That margin is almost entirely a function of specialty film mix. If EMBLEM HG volumes slip as packaging customers source alternatives, the margin reverts toward the segment mean and the valuation case collapses.

Third: glass-fiber chip-substrate volumes. Performance Materials reported operating profit up 251.7% year-on-year in the nine-month period, driven by what the company described as "significant growth" in ultra-thin Low CTE and E Glass Fabrics for high-end mobile memory applications. The DIC partnership announced in December 2025 for PPS film targeting millimetre-wave radar and next-generation communications PCBs is the most forward-looking data point in the portfolio. Neither the revenue nor the margin from that programme has been disaggregated; it should be by the FY3/27 Q1 release in August.

## Red Lights

The failure case is more mechanical. Unitika's five-year target posits ¥70 billion in revenue by FY3/29 with ¥6.5 billion in operating profit — implying a 9.3% margin on a structurally smaller base. If FY3/26 full-year operating profit undershoots ¥9.5 billion, the trajectory to that target requires acceleration in every subsequent year. More critically: if revenue falls materially below ¥110 billion — the guided -13% decline driven entirely by the divestiture scope change — it would indicate that remaining businesses are also losing volume, not merely shedding commodity tonnage.

An equity ratio of 25.2% as of December 2025, up from a precarious 10.4% a year earlier, provides breathing room; but that expansion is almost entirely REVIC's ¥20 billion Class C injection and the ¥44.5 billion cash build from asset sales. The underlying business has not yet earned its way to solvency. Any fresh impairment charge — the FY3/25 write-down was ¥37.9 billion — or a REVIC request to deploy additional capital beyond the committed ¥20 billion would signal that the cleaned-up balance sheet was a temporary construct, not a foundation.

## The One Ratio That Decides Everything

The lever that matters most is not revenue, not margin, not net income — it is the ratio of specialty and electronics revenue to commodity revenue. In FY3/25 terms, that meant comparing High Polymer's ¥55.4 billion (mostly specialty, 8.5% growth) and Functional Materials' ¥37.0 billion (8.3% growth) against Fiber's ¥33.9 billion (2.8% growth, loss-making). By FY3/27, with fibers largely divested, the comparison becomes Polymers plus Performance Materials electronics applications versus the residual commodity base within those segments. Watch for Unitika to begin disclosing an electronics-materials revenue sub-line in forthcoming REVIC progress reports; if it doesn't, assume the mix shift is not outrunning expectations.

A two-year window to prove a 137-year-old company can become a specialty-materials maker — funded by the Japanese state's revitalization arm, watched by its main banks, and led by the first career engineer ever promoted to its presidency.
